usage: The standard polite way to ask someone's occupation; note the particle is 이, not 가.
바꾸다 = swap one thing for another; use it for switching careers, not just today's task.
전문 (專門, specialty) marks a skilled profession like doctor or lawyer.
없다, not 안 있다; this is the natural way to say 'unemployed' softly.
examples: 직업이 뭐예요?
What is your job?
The go-to first-meeting question; the verb is hidden inside 뭐예요.
제 직업은 간호사예요.
My job is a nurse.
Topic 직업은 + the profession + 예요; you name the job, you don't 'do' it.
좋은 직업을 갖고 싶어요.
I want to have a good occupation.
갖다(가지다) 'to hold/have' pairs with 직업 when talking about aspirations.
nuance: 직업 (職業, 'duty-work') is the abstract category of one's profession or line of work — the answer to 'what do you do for a living,' not the daily grind itself. The dividing line you must feel: 직업 is the occupation as an identity (간호사, 교사), 직장 is the specific company you belong to, and 일/업무 is the actual work you perform. So 직업이 뭐예요? asks WHAT you are, while 무슨 일 해요? asks more casually what work you do day to day. Register is neutral-to-formal, perfect for a first meeting; among close friends 무슨 일 해? feels warmer. The classic English-speaker trap is 직업을 해요 to mean 'I work' — Korean never 'does' an occupation; you simply state it with 이에요/예요 (선생님이에요), and the particle after 직업 is 이 (직업이), since the word ends in a consonant.

mistakes: Saying 직업을 해요 for 'I work' — you cannot 'do' an occupation in Korean. Name the job instead: 저는 요리사예요 (I'm a cook).
Confusing 직업 (the profession/identity) with 직장 (the workplace/company). '회사가 멀어요' uses 직장, but '의사예요' is your 직업.
Using 가 after 직업 (직업가) — because 직업 ends in a consonant, the subject particle is 이: 직업이 뭐예요?

usage: 회사 sits in front as a noun modifier; no particle needed between them.
한테 marks the human recipient of the question; 에게 is its formal twin.
Place + 직원 names the staff of a specific business.
뽑다 literally 'to pull/pick out' is the everyday verb for hiring.
examples: 저는 은행 직원이에요.
I am a bank employee.
Workplace + 직원 + 이에요 states your role simply.
직원한테 물어보세요.
Please ask a staff member.
You hear this constantly in shops; 한테 + 물어보다 = ask (a person).
이 가게는 직원이 친절해요.
The staff at this shop are kind.
직원이 + adjective; Korean keeps it singular even for 'the staff' collectively.
nuance: 직원 (職員, 'duty-personnel') is the plain, everyday word for anyone who works at a company, shop, bank, or office — the person on the other side of the counter helping you. The synonym contrast to nail: 직원 is generic 'staff' regardless of rank, while 사원 (社員) specifically names the entry-level rung on the corporate ladder, and 종업원 sounds older/more clerical (waitstaff, hired help). In daily life 직원 is overwhelmingly the natural choice — 직원한테 물어보세요 (ask a staff member) is a sentence you'll use weekly. Register is neutral and safe for everyone. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, don't call the customer a 직원 — the 직원 is the one who WORKS there, not the visitor (that's 손님); second, English says 'I asked the staff' with no particle, but Korean must mark the person with 한테/에게: 직원에게 물어봤어요.

Dropping the particle: 직원 물어봤어요 is wrong. You must mark the person you asked with 한테/에게 → 직원한테 물어봤어요.
Assuming 직원 means a high-ranked person. It's rank-neutral; the boss is 사장 or 상사, not just 직원.

usage: to be employed; to go to work regularly
다니다 'attend regularly' is the set verb; this whole phrase means 'have a job.'
직장 + 동료 (同僚, fellow worker) — your colleague at the same company.
to look for / find a job
구하다 'to seek/obtain' is the natural verb for job-hunting.
work life; life as an employee
생활 (生活, daily life) added to mean the whole experience of being employed.
examples: 저는 직장에 다녀요.
I have a job (I go to work).
직장에 다니다 = be employed; the 에 marks the place you regularly attend.
직장이 집에서 멀어요.
My workplace is far from home.
직장이 + 멀다; here 직장 means the physical workplace.
새 직장을 구하고 있어요.
I'm looking for a new job.
새 (new) directly modifies 직장; 구하다 = seek/find.
nuance: 직장 (職場, 'duty-place') literally means the 'place of one's work' and covers both the physical workplace and the broader fact of being employed. The crucial contrast: 직업 is your profession/identity (what you are — a teacher), while 직장 is the specific organization you belong to (where you work — Samsung). So 직장에 다니다, literally 'attend a workplace,' is THE idiomatic way to say 'I have a job,' built with 다니다 (to go regularly), the same verb used for 학교에 다니다 (attend school). A salaried worker is a 직장인. Register is neutral and extremely common. The big English-speaker pitfall is the verb: don't say 직장에 가다 to mean 'I'm employed' — 가다 only describes today's single trip to the office, whereas 다니다 captures the ongoing state of holding a job. Also resist the literal 'I have a job' = 직장을 가지다; Koreans say 직장에 다녀요 instead.

usage: 신입 (新入, newly entered) + 사원 — the fresh recruit, hired every spring.
to join as an entry-level employee
으로 marks the rank you enter AT; 입사하다 = enter a company.
정규 (正規, regular) contrasts with 계약직 (contract worker).
평 (平, plain/flat) stresses 'just a regular worker,' no title.
examples: 저는 신입 사원이에요.
I am a new employee.
신입 사원 is a fixed compound; + 이에요 states your level.
사원으로 입사했어요.
I joined as an entry-level employee.
으로 marks the entering rank; 입사하다 = enter the company, past 입사했어요.
대리로 승진하기 전에는 사원이었어요.
Before being promoted to 대리, I was a 사원.
Shows the rank ladder: 사원 → 대리; 이었어요 = was.
nuance: 사원 (社員, 'company-member') is specifically the BOTTOM formal rung on the Korean corporate title ladder — the rank a fresh hire holds before climbing to 대리 → 과장 → 차장 → 부장. The contrast you must internalize: 직원 is the generic, everyday word for 'staff' at any rank, whereas 사원 is a precise rank-title used mostly in HR and on org charts. So every 사원 is a 직원, but a 부장 (department head) is a 직원 and NOT a 사원. You'll hear 신입 사원 (new recruit) everywhere during 공채 (open hiring season). Register is formal/official. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 사원 just because you mean 'an employee' in casual conversation — say 직원. And note the particle 으로 in 사원으로 입사하다 marks the rank you enter as, an 'as/in the capacity of' meaning English drops entirely.

Thinking a manager (부장/과장) is a 사원. Those are higher ranks; 사원 is the lowest rung only.
Saying 사원에 입사하다. The rank you enter AS takes 으로: 사원으로 입사했어요.

usage: to attend to / handle one's work
보다 'to see/handle' is the set verb for processing duties, esp. office/admin work.
업무 + 시간; the time block during which work or service is done.
많다 describes the volume of duties; 바쁘다 describes you being busy.
to take charge of a task
맡다 'to be entrusted with' = be assigned a duty or responsibility.
examples: 오늘은 업무가 많아요.
I have a lot of work today.
업무가 + 많다; describes the amount of work, not your feelings.
업무 시간은 9시부터 6시까지예요.
Working hours are from 9 to 6.
업무 시간 + 부터...까지 frames the start and end of the workday.
새로운 업무를 맡게 됐어요.
I've been assigned a new task.
맡다 + 게 되다 = ended up being entrusted with; sounds natural for new duties.
nuance: 업무 (業務, 'occupation-affairs') is the formal word for the specific duties, tasks, and functions tied to a job — the work content itself, especially in office and administrative settings. The synonym contrast to feel: 일 is the broad, native, casual word for 'work/thing/matter' you'd use with friends (일이 많아 = so much to do), while 업무 is its Sino-Korean, businesslike counterpart used in emails, reports, and with superiors (업무 협조 부탁드립니다). They overlap, but 업무 carries an official, structured tone; you would not say 업무 for chores at home. The fixed verb 업무를 보다 ('handle work') mirrors 일을 보다 and 볼일을 보다 (run an errand). The English-speaker pitfall: don't say 업무를 가다 — you 업무를 보다/하다 (handle/do work), never 'go' work; and in relaxed conversation reaching for 업무 instead of 일 can sound stiff and over-formal, like saying 'attend to my duties' to a buddy.

Using 업무 in casual chat where 일 fits. To a friend say 일이 많아, not 업무가 많아 — the latter sounds like a memo.
Confusing 업무 (the tasks/duties) with 직업 (the profession). Your 업무 is what you do daily; your 직업 is what you are.

usage: 에서 marks the LOCATION where an action takes place (a meeting happens there).
예약하다 (豫約, reserve in advance) — the verb for booking rooms, tables, tickets.
비다 'be empty' + 어 있다 (resultant state) = currently available.
대 (大, big) prefixed; contrast 소회의실 (小, small room).
examples: 회의실에서 회의가 있어요.
There is a meeting in the meeting room.
회의실에서 + 있다; the meeting (회의) happens IN the room (회의실).
회의실을 예약했어요.
I booked the meeting room.
회의실을 + 예약하다, past 예약했어요; 을 marks the room as the object reserved.
지금 회의실이 비어 있어요?
Is the meeting room free right now?
비어 있다 = is (currently) empty/available — a natural way to check.
nuance: 회의실 (會議室, 'meeting-room') is built transparently from 회의 (a meeting) + 실 (room) — and that 실 is a powerful building block: once you know it, you recognize 사무실 (office), 화장실 (restroom), 교실 (classroom), and 연구실 (lab/study). The key contrast learners blur is 회의 vs 회의실: 회의 is the EVENT (the meeting), 회의실 is the PLACE (the room) — 회의실에서 회의를 해요 means 'we hold a meeting in the meeting room,' two different words. A near-synonym is 미팅룸 (a borrowed English term used in some modern offices), but 회의실 is the standard, safe word. Register is neutral/workplace. The sharpest English-speaker pitfall is the particle: an action OCCURS at 회의실에서 (dynamic location), not 회의실에 (static existence/destination). 회의실에 있어요 = 'it is IN the meeting room'; 회의실에서 일해요 = 'I work IN the meeting room.' Choosing 에 vs 에서 wrong is the classic beginner slip.

Using 에 for an action: 회의실에 회의해요 is wrong. Actions happen at 회의실에서; 에 is only for existence/destination.
Forgetting the 실 = room logic and inventing words. The pattern 회의+실, 사무+실, 화장+실 is consistent — lean on it.

usage: 직장 (workplace) + 상사; specifies a boss in the work context.
보고하다 (報告, report) + 한테 marking the person you report TO.
직속 (直屬, directly attached) = the boss right above you in the chain.
지시 (指示, directive); 의 links the superior to their command.
examples: 제 상사는 정말 친절해요.
My boss is really kind.
상사는 + adjective; used when TALKING ABOUT the boss, not addressing them.
상사한테 먼저 보고해야 해요.
I have to report to my boss first.
상사한테 + 보고하다; 한테 = to (a person); 야 하다 = have to.
새 상사가 오셨어요.
A new boss has arrived.
Honorific 오시다→오셨어요 shows respect for the superior's action.
nuance: 상사 (上司, 'upper-office/superior') is the general, descriptive term for anyone who outranks you at work, whatever their specific title. The vital register caution: 상사 is a word you use ABOUT your boss when describing them to others (우리 상사는…), almost never TO their face — addressing them directly, you must use their title + 님: 부장님, 팀장님, 과장님. Calling someone '상사님' to their face sounds odd, like addressing a teacher as 'Superior.' The opposite pole is 부하 ((部下), a subordinate), and a near-synonym 윗사람 ('person above') is softer/more general and can extend beyond work to any senior. Contrast also with 선배, who joined before you but isn't necessarily your boss. The English-speaker pitfall: English freely says 'my boss' and even addresses them by first name, but Korean hierarchy forbids both — you neither say 상사님 nor use their bare name; you use title + 님. Also mark the person you report to with 한테/에게, not just a bare noun.

Confusing 상사 (a superior person) with 회사 (the company). They sound similar but mean boss vs. corporation.

usage: 회사 (company) + 선배 — someone who joined before you, not necessarily your boss.
Add 님 to address a 선배 respectfully to their face.
한테 marks the source you learn FROM; 배우다 = learn.
대학 (university) + 선배 — an older schoolmate from the same university.
examples: 회사 선배가 많이 도와줬어요.
A senior at work helped me a lot.
선배가 + 도와주다 (help, with benefit); past 도와줬어요.
선배님, 이것 좀 알려 주세요.
Senior, please show me this.
Direct address 선배님 + 알려 주세요 (kindly tell/show me).
저는 그 선배를 정말 존경해요.
I really respect that senior.
선배를 + 존경하다 (respect); 를 marks the object of respect.
nuance: 선배 (先輩, 'earlier-generation/fellow') means someone senior to you who entered the same school, university, company, or field BEFORE you — a relationship that structures enormous amounts of Korean social life. The sharp contrast: a 선배 is defined by entering EARLIER, while a 상사 is defined by RANK — your 선배 may or may not be your boss, and your boss may not be your 선배 if they transferred in. Also distinguish 선배 from 어른 (an elder/adult by age generally). Unlike 상사, you CAN and do address a 선배 directly, adding 님 for politeness: 선배님. A 선배 traditionally looks after their 후배 (junior), often picking up the meal tab. Register: warm but respectful, deeply tied to hierarchy. The English-speaker pitfall: English has no real equivalent and learners default to 'senior' = 'boss' — but 선배 is about timing, not authority; treating every 선배 as a 상사 (or vice versa) misreads the relationship. Mark whom you learn from with 한테/에게.

선배 = 先輩, literally 'earlier-generation/fellow.'

English has no real equivalent and learners default to 'senior' = 'boss' — but 선배 is about timing, not authority; treating every 선배 as a 상사 (or vice versa) misreads the relationship. Mark whom you learn from with 한테/에게.

mistakes: Equating 선배 with 'boss.' A 선배 joined before you but may hold no authority; a boss with power is a 상사.
Confusing 선배 (joined before you) with 후배 (joined after you). They are mirror opposites — get the direction right.
Dropping 님 when speaking TO a senior. To their face it's 선배님; bare 선배 in direct address can sound too casual.

usage: 회사 + 후배 — someone who joined the company after you.
가르치다 = teach; seniors often guide their 후배.
to treat a junior (buy for them)
한테 marks the receiver; 사 주다 = buy (for someone's benefit).
대학 + 후배 — a younger schoolmate from the same university.
examples: 저는 후배가 한 명 있어요.
I have one junior.
후배가 + 한 명 (one person) + 있다; 명 is the counter for people.
후배한테 커피를 사 줬어요.
I bought my junior a coffee.
후배한테 + 사 주다, past 사 줬어요; the 줬 shows you did it FOR them.
그 후배는 일을 정말 잘해요.
That junior is really good at their work.
후배는 + 일을 잘하다 (be good at work).
nuance: 후배 (後輩, 'later-generation/fellow') is the mirror image of 선배: someone who entered the same school, company, or field AFTER you, regardless of their age in some cases (entry timing usually outweighs age). The contrast to keep straight is purely directional — 선배 = earlier, 후배 = later — and neither word is about workplace RANK (that's 상사 vs 부하). Within Korea's senior-junior culture, the 선배 is expected to look after the 후배: guiding them at work, answering questions, and famously treating them to meals or coffee (후배한테 밥 사 주다). Register: friendly and caring, but still hierarchy-aware. The key English-speaker pitfall is honorifics: you do NOT attach 님 to 후배 — 님 elevates seniors, so '후배님' is unnatural; you address a junior by name or with 씨. Many learners over-apply 님 to everyone out of caution, which actually misfires here. Also, don't assume a 후배 is younger or lower-ranked — they're simply LATER to the group.

usage: to go on a business trip
가다 is the set verb; you GO on a 출장, you don't 'do' one.
중 (中, in the middle of) + 이다 = currently on the trip.
해외 (海外, overseas) + 출장 — a trip abroad for work.
to return from a business trip
에서 marks the place you come back FROM; 돌아오다 = come back.
examples: 내일 부산으로 출장을 가요.
I'm going to Busan on a business trip tomorrow.
Place + 으로 (toward) + 출장을 가다; 으로 marks the direction.
부장님은 지금 출장 중이세요.
The manager is away on business now.
출장 중 + honorific 이세요 to respect the superior.
이번 출장은 일정이 빡빡해요.
This business trip has a tight schedule.
일정 (schedule) + 빡빡하다 (tight/packed) — a real coworker's complaint.
nuance: 출장 (出張, 'go-out-stretch/dispatch') means being sent away from your usual workplace to do work elsewhere — typically a trip to another city or country, often with an overnight stay. The synonym contrast that matters: 출장 is travel FOR WORK, sharply distinct from 여행 (a leisure trip) — never call a vacation a 출장. Within work travel, contrast 출장 (a farther/longer dispatch, often overnight) with 외근 (外勤, off-site work done and returned within the same day, like visiting a client across town). The set verb is 가다 (출장을 가다, go on a trip) and the status phrase is 출장 중이에요 (away on business). Register: standard workplace vocabulary. The English-speaker pitfall is the verb choice — learners say 출장을 하다 ('do a business trip') by analogy with English 'take/do,' but Korean uses 가다 (go); and direction takes 으로 (부산으로 출장 가요), not just 에. Also don't confuse the noun-internal 장 here (dispatch) with the 장 in 직장/공장 (place).

usage: 보다 'to see' is the FIXED verb here, exactly like 시험을 보다 (take an exam).
합격하다 (合格, pass) + 에 marking the interview you pass; opposite is 떨어지다 (fail).
면접 + 준비 (準備, preparation) — getting ready for the interview.
1차 (1次, first round); Korean hiring often has 1차, 2차 면접 stages.
examples: 내일 면접을 봐요.
I have a job interview tomorrow.
면접을 보다 → present 봐요; literally 'see an interview' = have one.
면접 준비를 열심히 했어요.
I prepared hard for the interview.
면접 준비 + 하다, past 했어요; 열심히 = diligently.
면접에 합격해서 정말 기뻐요.
I'm so happy I passed the interview.
면접에 합격하다 + ~아서 (reason) + 기쁘다 (glad).
nuance: 면접 (面接, 'face-contact/meet') literally means meeting face-to-face, and refers to the job interview where you sit before evaluators. The most important thing to lock in is the FIXED verb: 면접을 보다, literally 'to see an interview,' which uses the same 보다 as 시험을 보다 (take a test) — Korean treats undergoing an evaluation as 'seeing' it. The synonym contrast: 면접 is the oral, face-to-face interview, while 시험 (試驗) is a written test/exam, and 면담 (面談) is a softer counseling-style talk (e.g., with a professor), not a hiring screen. After a 면접 you hope to 합격하다 (pass) rather than 떨어지다 (fall/fail) or 불합격하다. Register: neutral, used in any job-search context. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 하다: 면접을 하다 sounds off from the candidate's side — you 면접을 보다 (take it); the company that conducts it may 면접을 진행하다. Also note you pass 면접에 (with 에), patterning like 시험에 합격하다.

usage: 쓰다 'to write' is the natural verb; you write a resume, you don't 'make' it.
내다 'to put/hand out' = submit; 이력서를 제출하다 is its formal twin.
에 marks WHERE you write; 적다 = jot/note down onto the document.
이력서 + 사진 — the ID-style photo traditionally attached in Korea.
examples: 이력서를 쓰고 있어요.
I'm writing my resume.
이력서를 + 쓰다 + 고 있다 (ongoing) → 쓰고 있어요.
회사에 이력서를 냈어요.
I submitted my resume to the company.
회사에 (to the company) + 이력서를 내다, past 냈어요.
이력서에 경력을 자세히 적었어요.
I wrote my work experience on the resume in detail.
이력서에 + 경력 (career) + 적다, past 적었어요.
nuance: 이력서 (履歷書, 'tread-history-document') literally means a 'record-of-what-you've-walked' document — the page listing your education, work history, and qualifications when applying for a job. The key contrast to draw: 이력서 is the structured factual resume (dates, schools, jobs in fields), whereas 자기소개서 (自己紹介書), often shortened to 자소서, is the separate, longer SELF-INTRODUCTION essay where you narrate your motivation and personality — Korean applications almost always require BOTH, so never use them interchangeably. The verbs are 쓰다 (write it) then 내다/제출하다 (submit it). A culturally specific point: a traditional Korean 이력서 includes a small formal 이력서 사진 (ID photo). Register: neutral job-search vocabulary. The English-speaker pitfall: don't say 이력서를 만들다 ('make/craft a resume') — Korean uses 쓰다 (write), because a resume is conceived as written text, not a manufactured object; and remember that what English calls a 'cover letter' maps roughly onto 자기소개서, not 이력서.

usage: 높다 'be high' is the adjective for salary level — NOT 비싸다 (expensive).
올리다 'to raise' (transitive); the intransitive 'salary rises' is 연봉이 오르다.
협상 (協商, negotiation) — the talk where you settle your yearly pay.
How much is the annual salary?
얼마 asks the amount; a direct (somewhat blunt) money question.
examples: 이 회사는 연봉이 높아요.
This company's salary is high.
연봉이 + 높다; salary takes 높다/낮다 (high/low), not 비싸다.
올해 연봉이 조금 올랐어요.
My salary went up a little this year.
연봉이 + 오르다 (rise, intransitive), past 올랐어요.
입사할 때 연봉 협상을 했어요.
I negotiated my salary when I joined.
입사할 때 (when joining) + 연봉 협상을 하다, past 했어요.
nuance: 연봉 (年俸, 'year-stipend') is your pay expressed as a YEARLY total — and crucially, this is the default unit Koreans use to discuss and compare pay (연봉 3천 = 30 million won a year), unlike the English habit of quoting an hourly or monthly figure. The essential contrast: 연봉 is the annual gross figure used in offers and negotiations, while 월급 (月給, 'month-pay') is the monthly paycheck you actually take home each month — mixing them up distorts the numbers twelvefold. Related: 시급 (時給) is hourly wage (for part-timers), and 보너스/성과급 are bonuses on top. A new hire goes through 연봉 협상 (salary negotiation). Register: neutral, though asking 연봉이 얼마예요? directly can feel intrusive with someone you don't know well. The big English-speaker pitfall is the adjective: a high salary is 연봉이 높다 (high), and a low one 낮다 (low) — NEVER 연봉이 비싸다 ('expensive'), because 비싸다 is for the price of goods, not for amounts of money like wages.

usage: 하다 turns the noun into the event; or just 승진하다 as one verb.
to be promoted to department head
Rank + 으로 (to/as) + 승진하다 marks the rank you rise TO.
빠르다 'be fast' describes the pace of climbing the ladder.
축하하다 (祝賀, congratulate); a set phrase when a coworker moves up.
examples: 이번에 승진을 했어요.
I got promoted this time.
승진을 하다, past 했어요; 이번에 = this time/round.
과장으로 승진했어요.
I was promoted to section chief.
Rank 과장 + 으로 + 승진하다, past 승진했어요.
승진 축하해요!
Congratulations on your promotion!
Fixed congratulation; just 승진 + 축하해요, no particle needed.
nuance: 승진 (昇進, 'rise-advance') means moving UP to a higher rank or title at work — climbing the corporate ladder from 사원 to 대리 to 과장 and beyond. The contrasts to keep distinct: 승진 is rising in RANK within a workplace, different from 합격 (passing an exam or interview to get IN), from 취직/취업 (landing a job in the first place), and from 이직 (changing to a different company). The verb is 승진하다, and to name the rank you rose to, use rank + 으로: 부장으로 승진했어요 (promoted to department head), where 으로 carries an 'into/as' meaning. When a colleague is promoted, the ready-made phrase is 승진 축하해요. Register: neutral, congratulatory. The English-speaker pitfall: English says 'I GOT a promotion,' tempting learners into 승진을 받다 ('receive a promotion') — but Korean treats it as something you DO/achieve: 승진을 하다 or simply 승진하다, not 받다. Also don't mark the new rank with 에 (부장에 승진 is wrong); the directional 으로 is required.
